performers: Marian Anderson, contralto; San Francisco Symphony Orchestra; Pierre Monteux, conductor
question: How does the second stanza change the opening’s familiar instrumental pattern?
intro: A mother enters a room, and the speaker’s gaze drops to the place where their child would normally be. Mahler sets the two related stanzas without violins, leaving cor anglais, other winds and lower strings unusually exposed. Marian Anderson and Pierre Monteux shape this alternative performance.

sections.label: First stanza · the empty threshold
sections.mNote: cor anglais and lower parts begin a closely woven texture

sections.label: Second stanza · the remembered entrance
sections.mNote: the opening returns with harp and pizzicato double bass

sections.label: Orchestral close · the opening recalled
sections.mNote: horns and bowed cellos change the opening’s colour

cues.title: The violins are absent
cues.text: Cor anglais and bassoons begin over plucked cellos. There are no violin parts anywhere in this song: listen to how the exposed wind lines and lower strings establish the colour before the singer joins them.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Song III, printed p. 33. Its instrumentation list omits violins; the opening staves identify cor anglais, bassoons and pizzicato cellos. This describes the opening passage, not a timed voice entrance.

cues.title: Looking below the mother’s face
cues.text: The speaker turns towards the entering mother, but first looks lower, at the place where the child’s face would have been. The poem locates absence in an ordinary movement of the eyes, before its final lament gives that loss a name.
cues.evidence: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-lied-3-wenn-dein-mutterlein/ Paraphrase of the first stanza and the final lament; not a subtitle aligned to a particular sung phrase.

cues.title: From separate lines to chords
cues.text: Across each stanza, compare the opening’s independently moving parts with the more chordal passages later on. The change lets a relatively simple vocal shape meet different kinds of accompaniment without becoming a wholly new melody.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 33–39 and the related second-stanza passage, pp. 40–46. The distinction is visible in the full score and discussed by Geert Woltjer: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html No exact change of texture is asserted at this timestamp.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Music for smaller halls
cues.text: Mahler gives the early performances in smaller halls in Vienna and Graz. The detailed scoring is not simply a large orchestra playing quietly: important lines are repeatedly entrusted to a few individual players.
cues.evidence: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm Scoring and performance-history notes identify the Kleiner Musikvereinsaal and Graz’s Stephaniesaal as the composer’s preferred early venues. This does not establish the ensemble size used for this recording.

cues.title: The opening returns with changes
cues.text: The second stanza brings back the opening cor anglais line. Harp and plucked double bass add a different foundation to the familiar pattern; compare this return with the cellos’ plucked pulse at the start.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 40, rehearsal 3. The report marks a boundary at 1:46, followed by a quieter recurring G–B–C pitch profile around 1:50–2:00. The cue describes the surrounding return; no instrumental attack or syllable is precisely aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The second stanza is not a copy
cues.text: As the second stanza unfolds, listen for shifts between the singer and the accompanying lines. Mahler preserves much of the first stanza’s design but redistributes details, so a familiar phrase can acquire another voice or register.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 43–46. Woltjer describes the exchanged melodic material in the second stanza: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html This is a passage-level comparison, not a claim about a particular attack.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Mahler reshapes Rückert’s poem
cues.text: Mahler changes the order of Rückert’s two stanzas and shortens the text. The version he sets begins with the gaze towards the threshold and ends with the image of a light of joy extinguished too soon.
cues.evidence: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html Describes reversal of Rückert’s stanzas, omission of part of the original first stanza and relocation of the final line. The resulting text is reproduced at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-lied-3-wenn-dein-mutterlein/.

cues.title: The opening changes its colour
cues.text: In the orchestral ending, cor anglais recalls the opening material, but horns and bowed cellos alter its support. The written close rests on G, the dominant of C minor, rather than returning to a settled C-minor final chord.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 47. The report marks 3:38 before the closing span and 3:50 within it; the final 4:00 window has G–B–D pitch classes. The score establishes the harmony; the report only corroborates its broad location.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The same outline gains a new foundation
transitions.how: After the first stanza’s descending close, the cor anglais recovers its initial line at the opening pace. Harp and pizzicato double bass now underpin the texture that the plucked cellos established at the start. The C-minor setting and familiar melody make the return clear, while the change in the lowest parts prevents an exact repetition.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 40, rehearsal 3, marked “Wie zu Anfang”. The 1:46 novelty point precedes the recurring opening pitch profile and a sustained quieter span at 1:50–2:05. The sung stanza itself begins later than this instrumental return.

transitions.title: The opening returns without its plucked bass
transitions.how: The vocal lament gives way to the opening cor anglais figure, now supported by horns and bowed cellos rather than the initial pizzicato cello pulse. The descending wind figures lengthen and the texture gradually loses motion. Its G-major close leaves C minor’s dominant standing, so the return of the opening melody does not bring a tonic conclusion.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 47, marked “Wieder wie zu Anfang”. The 3:38 boundary and lower onset density through 3:40–4:00 anchor the approximate coda span. The precise final vocal release has not been aligned.

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song III, printed pp. 33–47; no violins. These are passage-level scoring groups, not instantaneous lists of sounding parts. Timings are provisional score proportions checked against the audio report, without bar alignment or aural verification.

timeline.note: Opening: cor anglais and bassoon lines above the pizzicato cello pulse.
First-stanza opening: the voice joins a changing network of wind lines over the low pulse.
Return passage: harp and pizzicato double bass replace the opening cello foundation beneath the familiar wind figure.
Coda: horns and bowed cellos give the returning opening figure a different weight before its G-centred close.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
